topic: cold process soap: lye weighing, trace, gel phase in the mould, curing on the rack and lather

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-4)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: probe thermometer zapisujacy temperature wsadu; referent zwyczajny procesowy zakotwiczony poza rozmowa

base: I made my first cold process soap last week and the bars came out crumbly.
An older batch from the spring sits on the curing rack and looks fine.
A probe thermometer clipped to the pot logs the temperature right through the pour.
The new bars crumble at the edges and show white streaks inside the cut.
Is that too much lye, or did the batch simply seize in the pot?
White streaks usually mean the lye never mixed evenly into the oils.
Crumbly edges point the same way, since the outside sets before the centre does.
Blend with a stick blender until the batter traces evenly across the whole surface.
Weigh the lye again as well, because a scale error shows up exactly like this.
I reweighed everything and the lye was about twelve grams over the recipe.
The second batch traced properly and poured like thin custard into the mould.
The probe thermometer showed the batter climbing to sixty degrees inside the mould.
Is sixty degrees too warm, or is that the gel phase everyone mentions?
Sixty is the gel phase and it does no harm to the finished bar.
Gelled soap goes darker in the middle and often looks slightly translucent when cut.
Worry only above about seventy degrees, where the batter can crack or volcano.
Cover the mould with a board and leave it undisturbed for a full day.
The bars cut cleanly after a day and the colour is even throughout.
They feel soft, though, and my thumbnail marks them without any real effort.
The older batch on the rack is hard and rings when I tap it.
How long should these cure before they harden up like the older ones?
Give them six weeks on a rack with air moving freely around every bar.
Water leaves slowly, and a bar loses most of its softness in the first month.
Turn them onto a fresh face every week so no side stays damp underneath.
A bar that rings has cured properly and will last twice as long in use.
Six weeks on the rack and the bars now ring exactly as you said.
A few of them have developed orange spots scattered across the cut faces.
The spots smell faintly rancid when I hold a bar close to my nose.
Are those spots dangerous, or merely ugly on an otherwise usable bar?
They are harmless but they spread, and the smell grows stronger over the months.
Rancid spots come from oils that were already old when they went in.
Buy oils in small quantities and keep them dark and cool between batches.
Use the spotted bars for washing floors and let the clean ones age on.
I bought fresh oils and the last two batches have stayed completely clean.
The lather is thin, though, and disappears almost as soon as it forms.
My recipe is mostly olive oil with a little coconut and some tallow.
Should I raise the coconut, or will that make the bar too drying?
Raise the coconut to about a fifth and the lather will thicken noticeably.
Beyond a quarter it does dry the skin, especially in hard winter water.
Adding castor oil at five percent will hold the bubbles far longer as well.
Change one thing at a time and label every batch with its date.
